{"id": "39:18/q08", "question": "What do they follow as the best speech or course?", "turns_on": "Whether 'best' picks true speech, scripture, obedience, a superior lawful course or a specific confession.", "positions": [{"id": "39:18/q08/p1", "position": "Whatever is truest, most guiding and best supported.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī stresses oneness and obedience; al-Thaʿlabī and al-Ṭabrisī, truth-guiding speech; Ibn ʿAṭiyya favors broad discernment, encompassing the examples, as does al-Baghawī's conclusion that all given explanations are good. Al-Biqāʿī contrasts reason with desire; al-Rāghib says furthest from doubt; Ṭabāṭabāʾ includes truth over falsehood and greater over lesser guidance."}, {"id": "39:18/q08/p2", "position": "The Qur'an, preferred to other discourse.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and many others give this reading. Al-Biqāʿī says the Qur'an surpasses other good revealed books in expression, meaning and arrangement; Bursevī cites 39:23. Ibn Kathīr and Study Quran compare Moses' command to take the Torah's best at 7:145."}, {"id": "39:18/q08/p5", "position": "Pardon, forbearance, patience and discreet charity over lawful alternatives.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj cites 42:43 and 42:41; al-Kashshāf adds 2:237 and 2:271. Ṭabāṭabāʾ rejects restriction to such choices."}, {"id": "39:18/q08/p6", "position": "Obligations or strict duties over recommendations or dispensations, and recommendations over the merely permitted.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Qāshānī mention duties or strictness; al-Kashshāf, al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī include the more rewarding recommendation. Al-Rāzī's fuller prayer has opening intention, Fātiḥa, tranquility, tashahhud and salutation; Bursevī gives washing thrice and glorification."}, {"id": "39:18/q08/p7", "position": "The best report from a gathering, withholding its bad parts.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is transmitted by al-Māwardī, al-Kashshāf, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān; al-Nasafī gives the conversational use."}, {"id": "39:18/q08/p8", "position": "The confession that there is no god but God.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd and al-Qurṭubī apply this to the three early monotheists; Bursevī's Kashf al-Asrār applies it to Abū Bakr's listeners."}, {"id": "39:18/q08/p9", "position": "Islam after hearing Muslims and polytheists.", "reasons": "Al-Naqqāsh, reported by al-Māwardī, names this choice."}, {"id": "39:18/q08/p10", "position": "Revelation understood and put into practice.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr and Study Quran invoke Moses and 7:145; Iṣlāḥī says they follow every sound thing; Study Quran connects understanding with acting on revelation, citing 39:9 and 5:100."}, {"id": "39:18/q08/p11", "position": "Speech or action devoted solely to God, especially pure remembrance.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī gives both possibilities."}, {"id": "39:18/q08/p12", "position": "The best evidenced legal view or strongest proof in each science.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf applies examination to schools of law; Ibn ʿĀshūr and an attributed saying apply it to soundest argument and each field."}]}
{"id": "39:18/q09", "question": "Can Qur'anic passages be intrinsically better than one another?", "turns_on": "Whether superiority concerns divine speech itself, its topic, its reward or its application.", "positions": [{"id": "39:18/q09/p1", "position": "Yes, passages about God are superior by their subject.", "reasons": "Bursevī prefers the investigators' view: al-Ikhlāṣ names divine oneness and attributes while al-Masad's merit is God's speech. Another reported view makes Qur'anic pardon, forgiveness or patience better depending on the actor."}]}
{"id": "39:18/q10", "question": "What does God's guidance of them consist in?", "turns_on": "How divine agency, human receptivity and human action relate.", "positions": [{"id": "39:18/q10/p1", "position": "God guides them to religion, truth and what pleases Him.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Bayḍāwī say His religion; al-Ṭabrisī says they follow guidance to truth; al-Qurṭubī says what pleases Him; Ibn Kathīr extends it through this world and the next; Iṣlāḥī links a truth-loving attitude to God's gift."}, {"id": "39:18/q10/p2", "position": "God causes guidance; the soul receives it but cannot originate the decisive preference.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī argues equal receptivity to true and false belief cannot itself select one, like a body receptive to motion and rest; appeal to will repeats the problem. Al-Ālūsī reports the Ashʿarī divine-act-and-acceptance position; al-Bayḍāwī also names both sides."}, {"id": "39:18/q10/p3", "position": "God creates souls receptive to the Prophet's guidance, beyond sending commands available to everyone.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says even rejecters received commands; these listeners sought God's approval and rescue. {"id": "39:18/q11", "question": "Why does the first closing clause name God and use a demonstrative?", "turns_on": "Whether emphasis falls on the recipients or on the divine guide.", "positions": [{"id": "39:18/q11/p1", "position": "The demonstrative and defined terms single out deserving recipients of guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says demonstratives after descriptions emphasize a judgment, citing 38:55; the two definite terms restrict this additional guidance compared with the losers of 39:15."}, {"id": "39:18/q11/p2", "position": "Naming God magnifies the guidance and shows access to Him is through Him.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī compares 6:90; here the object of guidance is explicit and the relative clause repeats it."}]}
{"id": "39:18/q12", "question": "What makes them people of understanding?", "turns_on": "Whether intellect is identified by action, freedom from distortion or inward receptivity.", "positions": [{"id": "39:18/q12/p1", "position": "They possess and use sound intellect to follow truth and divine commands.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī glosses understanding; Muqātil joins it to obeying commands and avoiding prohibitions; al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Nasafī stress using reason. Ibn Kathīr adds upright disposition; Ṭabāṭabāʾ calls following truth its sign; Study Quran cites 39:9 and 5:100 for acting on revelation."}, {"id": "39:18/q12/p2", "position": "Their intellect is free from fancy, habit, delusion and caprice.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī describe freedom from these influences. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites Khadīja, Abū Bakr and ʿAlī believing at the first call; Kur'an Yolu reports al-Rāzī that strong intellect is needed to assemble true knowledge."}, {"id": "39:18/q12/p3", "position": "Their liberated inner cores discern promptings and receive verified meanings.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī speaks of original guidance and liberated cores; al-Qushayrī distinguishes impulses of self, Satan, angel and the Real, each calling for a different response."}]}
{"id": "39:18/q13", "question": "What do the repeated demonstrative and pronoun add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:18/q13/p1", "position": "They honor these people and specify their fully rooted understanding.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says repetition and 'they' intensify honor and restrict true intellect to clear minds. {"id": "39:18/q15", "question": "What inward or prophetic significance is given to the best address?", "turns_on": "Whether excellence concerns prophetic rank or spiritually helpful company.", "positions": [{"id": "39:18/q15/p1", "position": "Muhammad has the best prophetic address and primordial spiritual precedence.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī says all prophets teach good but Muhammad leads each rank; a prophetic report calls his community last in worldly time but first in primordial address and the holy station."}, {"id": "39:18/q15/p2", "position": "The best companion recalls God by appearance and the afterlife by deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī transmits Jesus' description."}]}
{"id": "39:18/q16", "question": "What reports illustrate selecting excellent speech?", "turns_on": "The reports have different speakers and events.", "positions": [{"id": "39:18/q16/p1", "position": "Abū al-Dardāʾ prized thirst in heat, night prostration and companions selecting speech like choice dates.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Ṭabrisī transmit this triad."}, {"id": "39:18/q16/p2", "position": "Al-Kalbī prized prostration, companions choosing good words like fruit and striving for God.", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits this differing triad."}, {"id": "39:18/q16/p3", "position": "A herald promised Paradise to those dying without shirk, then ʿUmar recalled him for fear of complacency.", "reasons": "Abū Saʿīd reports the Prophet contrasting hope in mercy and fear of punishment."}, {"id": "39:18/q16/p4", "position": "The verse followed an unidentified group's statement.", "reasons": "Al-Durr's excerpt preserves neither their identity nor their words."}]}
{"id": "39:18/q17", "question": "How does the verse connect to its neighbors and earlier scripture?", "turns_on": "Which nearby promise or scriptural parallel explains this statement.", "positions": [{"id": "39:18/q17/p1", "position": "It completes glad tidings to those who reject false worship, unlike people bound for Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī preserve continuity with 39:17; Iṣlāḥī contrasts the believers with those beyond the Prophet's responsibility. {"id": "39:18/q18", "question": "How do Arabic comparison forms treat qualities of mind?", "turns_on": "Whether a quality describes mental character or bodily form.", "positions": [{"id": "39:18/q18/p1", "position": "Mental traits admit exclamatory comparison because they concern character and discernment.", "reasons": "Sībawayh permits ما أحمقه, ما أرعنه, ما أنوكه, ما ألده and ما أهوجه and compares these to foolishness and courage."}, {"id": "39:18/q18/p2", "position": "Colors and bodily defects do not form these Afʿal comparisons and exclamations.", "reasons": "Sībawayh uses ما أشد حمرته and extends restriction to أفعل به and أفعل منه; al-Khalīl likens such traits to body parts. {"id": "39:18/q19", "question": "How are reports distinguished from an author's linguistic analysis?", "turns_on": "Whether a source transmits a report or endorses its analysis.", "positions": [{"id": "39:18/q19/p1", "position": "Ibn Jinnī marks where Abū ʿAlī's report ends and his own analysis starts.", "reasons": "He uses formulas introducing his independent position."}, {"id": "39:18/q19/p2", "position": "Ibn Jinnī trusts Ibn Mujāhid's transmission while opposing his linguistic judgment.", "reasons": "The note separates reports and readings from their interpreter's reasoning."}]}

{"id": "39:21/q03", "question": "What is the water's origin and its relation to springs?", "turns_on": "The accounts differ over current rainfall, a primordial supply, or a physical source of spring water; reports and seasonal observations are used.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q03/p1", "position": "It is rain or other precipitation stored in earth and led into springs.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and others infer rain because springs swell with rain and dry without it (Ibn ʿAṭiyya); Abū Ḥayyān and al-Bursevī describe gradual release. Ibn Kathīr cites 25:48 and says God apportions differently sized springs; Saʿīd specifies mountain snow. Al-Ālūsī prefers rain and snow while allowing some condensation. Al-Mībudhī says seasonal evidence rules out vapor as sole source. Al-Biqāʿī stresses measured descent and reemergence."}, {"id": "39:21/q03/p2", "position": "All earthly water originally descended from heaven, sometimes reaching a rock before distribution.", "reasons": "Al-Shaʿbī, Saʿīd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Kalbī transmit the universal claim. Ibn ʿAbbās says underground veins alter its taste; ascending would sweeten salt water. Abū Hurayra's prophetic report places sweet waters and pollinating winds beneath Jerusalem's rock; al-Bursevī says clouds convey water there. Al-Ālūsī allows the Ibn ʿAbbās report literally if authentic and marfūʿ; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the rain and spring explanations close."}, {"id": "39:21/q03/p3", "position": "At creation water descended from the Sea of the Throne onto a waterless earth.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports and rejects it: no sound report supports it, and the general invitation to see could not mean unwitnessed creation without forcing an implausibly exclusive address to the Prophet."}, {"id": "39:21/q03/p4", "position": "The water comes from underground veins rather than descending from the sky.", "reasons": "Al-Durr's wording attributes this to Ibn ʿAbbās, with the ascent challenge; other transmissions of Ibn ʿAbbās explicitly say the opposite."}, {"id": "39:21/q03/p5", "position": "Underground vapor condenses and bursts through earth as springs.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the philosophers. Sharḥ al-Mawāqif allows vapor but prefers accumulated water because springs rise with snow and rain. Abū al-Barakāt rejects vapor as a sole cause since it predicts the opposite seasonal pattern; al-Mībudhī says this does not exclude partial contribution."}, {"id": "39:21/q03/p6", "position": "Scattered water matter deep underground joins and forms spring water.", "reasons": "Sharḥ al-Mawāqif finds this stronger than condensed vapor on the evidence of well and spring levels responding to snow and rain."}]}
{"id": "39:21/q04", "question": "What does 'sky' denote?", "turns_on": "Whether it names rain's immediate direction or remote celestial causes.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q04/p1", "position": "It is the direction above.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī rejects direct fall from the familiar celestial sphere: clouds and heavy rain may lie below a mountain observer."}, {"id": "39:21/q04/p2", "position": "It names celestial bodies as remote causes of rain.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the sun drawing vapor upward and changing positions leading to cloud formation."}]}
{"id": "39:21/q05", "question": "What does 'salakahu' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb emphasizes insertion and underground passage or the ensuing outflow.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q05/p1", "position": "God inserts, conducts and orders water through earth into springs, wells and channels.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba describes entry into earth; Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites poetry for driving through; al-Jishumī compares threading a needle and distinguishes salakahu fīhi from salaka fī al-Islām. Al-Bursevī distinguishes salaka, leading in, from aslaka, inserting. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī and others compare courses to bodily veins; al-Qurṭubī cites 23:18 for settled water."}, {"id": "39:21/q05/p2", "position": "God makes water gush forth as springs.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī gives this as an alternative to sending water into the ground; al-Biqāʿī emphasizes its recurrence after being hidden in the depths."

{"id": "39:21/q06", "question": "What does 'yanābīʿ' mean and how is it formed?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural names outlets or their flowing contents.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q06/p1", "position": "It is the plural of yanbūʿ, a spring or outlet where water wells up.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj gives the yafʿūl pattern from nabʿ; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the formation intensive and says an ʿayn is one kind. Ibn Kaysān, via al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī, explains poetic yanbāʿ by lengthening yanbaʿ's fatḥa; al-Naḥḥās records yanbaʿ as a singular. Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ give three verb vocalizations via al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī."}, {"id": "39:21/q06/p2", "position": "It can denote the gushing water or a flowing thing.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī allows spring source or flowing water. Al-Ālūsī reports yānbiʿ, 'flowing thing', but finds its circumstantial parse awkward because min al-arḍ would be expected."}]}
{"id": "39:21/q07", "question": "How is 'yanābīʿ' parsed?", "turns_on": "The case is shared but its governing relation and implied words differ.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q07/p1", "position": "It is accusative after an omitted preposition: water is directed into springs.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, al-Bursevī and al-Ālūsī supply the preposition; al-Bursevī compares the explicit preposition in 28:32. Al-Ālūsī rejects a cognate accusative as requiring remote ellipsis."}, {"id": "39:21/q07/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial accusative for water becoming springs or flowing.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī and al-Bayḍāwī allow a state construction; al-Ālūsī finds the flowing-water version awkward with fī rather than min al-arḍ."}, {"id": "39:21/q07/p3", "position": "It is an adverbial accusative of place.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī and al-Bayḍāwī allow a locative parse."}, {"id": "39:21/q07/p4", "position": "It is a cognate accusative with an implied verbal noun or genitive.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī records and rejects both as distant ellipses."}]}
{"id": "39:21/q08", "question": "What does 'in the earth' attach to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q08/p1", "position": "It specifies the location of the springs.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī makes it a qualifier of yanābīʿ; al-Bursevī compares water being put in an irrigation channel in a garden."}]}
{"id": "39:21/q09", "question": "Why use 'then' and the imperfect for crop growth?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q09/p1", "position": "The sequence conveys delay between rain and growth, while the imperfect vividly presents the scene.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī identifies the temporal interval; al-Bursevī and al-Ālūsī allow delay in time or rank."}]}
{"id": "39:21/q10", "question": "What role does water play in crop production?", "turns_on": "Whether water is an instrument or merely accompanies God's act.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q10/p1", "position": "God brings crops forth by water as a divinely chosen means, without intrinsic necessity.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī distinguishes divine wisdom from water's independent necessity. {"id": "39:21/q11", "question": "What does 'zarʿ' cover?", "turns_on": "Whether the defining feature is cultivation or lack of a trunk.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q11/p1", "position": "It covers cultivated crops generally.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān include all crops; al-Bursevī says the original verbal noun for sowing or growth names the product here; al-Qurṭubī says the generic singular embraces many kinds."}, {"id": "39:21/q11/p2", "position": "It is trunkless vegetation, distinguished from trees.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguish shajar with trunk and branches, while nabāt includes both."}]}
{"id": "39:21/q12", "question": "What differs in the crop's 'colors'?", "turns_on": "Whether 'colors' denotes hues, kinds, or both with other properties.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q12/p1", "position": "The crop differs in visible hues.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj lists green, yellow, red and white; al-Qurṭubī adds blue and luminous or white; al-Baghawī gives red, yellow and green. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports a group choosing qualities. Al-Rāghib, via al-Bursevī, places yellow between black and white and notes that it may signify black."}, {"id": "39:21/q12/p2", "position": "It differs in kinds or species.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan b. Muslim is transmitted with varying patronymics, Ibn Bayān and Ibn Yannāq; examples include wheat, barley, sesame, rice and maize, with 16:13 cited. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports a group choosing kinds; Iṣlāḥī says alwān can mean types."}, {"id": "39:21/q12/p3", "position": "It embraces hues, species, and further qualities.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Bursevī name hues alongside crop kinds. Ibn Kathīr adds form, taste, scent and benefit; al-Biqāʿī adds temperament despite common water; al-Ālūsī extends it to all perceptible qualities, food and other crops. {"id": "39:21/q13", "question": "What does 'yahīju' mean?", "turns_on": "The word is applied to different growth or decay stages; rising can follow full drying.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q13/p1", "position": "The plant dries, withers, or reaches the limit of drying.", "reasons": "Al-Aṣmaʿī speaks of complete drying and recession. Al-Jawharī includes dry or yellowed fields, wind drying crops, and anger rising or calming. Al-Jishumī also lists motion, turmoil, stirred blood, sexual arousal and longing. Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī specify dryness's limit; Iṣlāḥī its beginning. {"id": "39:21/q22", "question": "What does the crop cycle teach about God's power and human duty?", "turns_on": "Different implications are emphasized: restoration, lordship, or gratitude and accountability.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q22/p1", "position": "God can restore the dead and fulfill His promise as He revives and changes plants.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says God can restore bodies and accidents in their former state; Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Biqāʿī and Asad infer resurrection. {"id": "39:21/q23", "question": "What does the cycle teach about worldly and human life?", "turns_on": "The applications stress transience, reception of revelation, or the general act of reflection.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q23/p1", "position": "Worldly beauty and human youth flourish briefly, then fade through old age to death.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Ibn al-Jawzī call it a worldly parable; al-Zamakhsharī cites 10:24 and 18:45, Ibn Kathīr 18:45, and Study Quran 18:45 and 57:20. {"id": "39:21/q24", "question": "How is the cycle read inwardly?", "turns_on": "Different correspondences use the image for spiritual cultivation, hypocrisy, annihilation, or fulfillment.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q24/p1", "position": "Spiritual water or knowledge enters inner faculties and produces varied deeds and morals.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī makes sky spirit, rain knowledge, springs wisdom in souls, and crops deeds and morals. {"id": "39:21/q25", "question": "How does the verse relate to the sūra and other verses?", "turns_on": "Contextual readings emphasize guidance, worldly transience, or promised rivers.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q25/p1", "position": "It resumes the guidance theme and prepares the guided and misguided responses of 39:22–23.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr traces the theme past an excursus at 39:2; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links lordship and guidance. {"id": "39:21/q26", "question": "What ancillary reports and lexical notes accompany the discussion?", "turns_on": "These are separate incidental reports, not competing versions of one event.", "positions": [{"id": "39:21/q26/p1", "position": "Companions wept and shivered at the Qur'an; Asmāʾ rejected listeners' fainting.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits Asmāʾ's refuge-seeking on hearing of fainting."}, {"id": "39:21/q26/p2", "position": "ʿAlī said he judged by the Qur'an alone when accused of unbelief and hypocrisy.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits his reply that he judged no created person."}, {"id": "39:21/q26/p3", "position": "A manuscript fragment vocalizes 'lā tablā', but its antecedent is missing.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevī mentions damma and fatḥa on the imperfect prefix and lām."}, {"id": "39:21/q26/p4", "position": "A lexical excursus distinguishes bodily illness from metaphorical illness of hearts.", "reasons": "Ibn Fāris roots marad in departure from health; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says legal usages mean bodily illness and heart illness extends the sense."}]}
